1 Make sure you are sitting in the driver’s seat.

About the only thing they get right, but really, where else would you be sitting to adjust the mirrors? If you are so dumb as to attempt to set the mirrors from any other position it is likely you are dumb enough to be a danger to yourself and everyone else on the public roads.

2 Move your seat so you are at a comfortable height and depth...your feet are gently resting on the pedals

Wrong...and wrong. Driving is about controlling the vehicle, NOT about your comfort.

a: Move the seat forward (or backwards) until your left foot can be firmly planted on the floor with your butt at the back and bottom of the seat. Almost all vehicles have a flat, raised and angled part on the left of the floor that is there for this purpose. Use your left foot to push your body back into the seat so that you are wedged into the seat while your left leg is almost fully extended. In evasive maneuvers if you cannot do this you will flop around and this will change your relation to the wheel and the brake pedal, making it more difficult to control the vehicle. Unless your legs are different lengths, you will still be able to reach the brake and gas pedal with your right foot. (Left foot braking is a different discussion).

If your seat can be raised or lowered, set it so you can see over the dash, and if your wheel tilts, tilt it up (or down) so it is a few inches above your lap. You should be able to see your instrument cluster through the wheel. Your goal here is to get as high up in the vehicle as possible, with the air bag in the steering wheel pointed right at the center of your chest.

Use a cushion to increase your height if you are particularly short and cannot see over the front of the car.

At this point if your seat has a tilt adjust (depends on your vehicle) adjust the tilt so the front of the seat just supports the back of your thighs.

b. Sit upright, no slouching! You are not on your couch watching Netflix, you are operating a 1-1/2 ton (or more) deadly weapon! Raise or lower the seat back until the headrest is less than an inch from your skull, AND at the same time raise or lower the head rest so the center of the head rest is nearest the bulge of your skull. (You'll thank me for this if your ever get rear ended, as even at an inch gap your skull will accelerate enough on impact to give yourself a nasty headache. I know this from experience. Further than that you may get a concussion). Some vehicles will have a rotating headrest to move it closer to your skull. Again, you want that less than an inch gap.

c: If your vehicle has lumbar adjustment (not all do) adjust it until the seat back makes firm contact with your back while you are sitting upright. If it does not and your lower back is not in contact, get a pillow thick enough so your back is firmly against the pillow and the seat back.

Now you are at the correct height and depth. On to the mirrors, but Parts 3-6 come later. First comes moving your rear-view mirror.

1 Sit in your normal comfortable correct driving posture.

See a-c above

2 Move the rear-view mirror so you can see the entire rear window.

Most (but not all) vehicles have two pivots on the windshield mounted mirror. Adjust the mirror so that the rear window completely fills the mirror. Almost all mirrors are of a shape and size to do this, specific to the vehicle. Using BOTH pivots, move the mirror so that the center of the lane directly behind you (in the mirror) is in the center of the mirror, and the mirror is as low as possible AND the entire rear window is seen in the mirror AND the horizon at the center is in the middle of the mirror.

3 Turn on the night-view setting to avoid glare

When you flip the lever to turn on the night-view be certain it flips down, not up. It is possible to aim the day-view right at the dome light and could be a problem at night should the dome light come on, blowing your night vision.

4 Flip the mirror upside down if you are over 6 feet (1.8 m) feet tall....the blind-spot...is substantially smaller.

Wrong. The blind spot is not in this mirror (or any other mirror). That is why it is called a blind spot, because those spots are not shown in a mirror.

Parts 3-4 Electric, manual, or by hand, are all the same procedure, #5

5 Adjust the left-right plane of the mirrors....to see the edge of the back of your car

Wrong. This method CREATES blind spots. As a vehicle comes up from behind you (on either side) it will leave the view of the center mirror as it enters the view of the wing mirror, and then it will leave the view of the wing mirror, but hasn't yet reached your peripheral vision. That gap is the blind spot and it happens on both sides. The smaller the vehicle the more likely it is that it is not visible to you while in this blind spot. The following almost completely removes the two blind spots.

You want to see as much as possible of the area behind your head, so you want the view on the right side of the drivers side wing mirror to just overlap with what you can see on the left side of your center (windshield mounted) mirror.

As you have already correctly adjusted the center mirror, note any object at the very left side of the center mirror, then adjust the driver side wing mirror so that same object is just on the right side of the wing mirror.

Repeat this for the passenger side wing mirror, note any object on the very right side of the center mirrors view and adjust the wing mirror so that same object is just visible on the left side of the wing mirror. What this does is provide nearly complete coverage on the passenger side (if you have a convex mirror it will say on it "objects appear closer") and reduces the blind spot on the drivers side to the point where the rear of the vehicle passing you is just leaving the view of the wing mirror as the front of that vehicle enters your peripheral vision.

One of the benefits of this method is at night. When a vehicle is passing you and the nose of that vehicle is just at the rear of your vehicle, the drivers side headlight of that vehicle will be reflected directly into your eyes, and as he comes alongside you, the passenger side headlight will be reflected directly into your eyes until the driver side headlight enters your peripheral vision.

Another benefit is that a vehicle directly behind you is NOT showing his headlights directly into your wing mirrors, but only into your center mirror (which is flipped to night-view). I use this simple geometry when I come up behind a vehicle in the passing lane, by positioning my driver side head lamp directly into his driver side wing mirror. This gets his attention and if he doesn't get out of the way, then he gets a blip of the high beams directly into his eyes. Rarely is this not effective.

At the end of all this is the reminder to always shoulder check. Always, always, always. It has saved me from a crash many times.
